title: Accounting of the soul
hook: a daily honest review of one's actions

segments.voice: Yesterday, Israel Salanter poured just a little water so the water-carrier would carry less. Your line was not pious at others' expense. Whose buckets did you notice? Today, a nightly look at your own day. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-four.

A shop owner closes up for the night. The door is locked, the sign is flipped, and before going home she sits down with the register and the receipts. What came in. What went out. Where the numbers don't match. Nobody watching her would call it dramatic. It's ten quiet minutes, and it's the reason the shop is still open next year. Jewish teachers of character took that end-of-day ledger and turned it inward. The same sitting down, the same honest columns, but the business is your own day: what you said, what you did, where the numbers don't match. They have a name for it, and it's today's word.
screen: `THE SHOP CLOSES FOR THE NIGHT.` → `THE RECEIPTS COME OUT.` → `THE LEDGER TURNS INWARD.`

segments.voice: Cheshbon hanefesh. Cheshbon is an accounting, a reckoning, the word on a bill. Hanefesh means of the soul. An accounting of the soul. Turn it four ways. First, a verse in Lamentations. It says: "Let us search and try our ways, and return to the LORD." Search and try. Not glance. The verse asks for a real look, the way you'd go through a drawer, not just open it. Second, a Talmud pun. In the book of Numbers there's an old song that begins, come to Heshbon, the name of a city. The Talmud, in tractate Bava Batra, hears the city's name as cheshbon, accounting, and reads the line as advice: come, let us make an accounting of the world, what a good deed costs against what it gains, what a wrong gains against what it costs. A place on a map becomes a habit of the heart. Third, daily, not yearly. The season before Yom Kippur is known for a great yearly accounting. Mussar teachers asked for something smaller and more often: a short review each day, often at night, before sleep. Small enough that a single sharp word doesn't get lost in a year of them. Fourth, honest, not harsh. A good bookkeeper doesn't scream at the receipts. She just writes down what's there. A cheshbon hanefesh is the same: no beating yourself up, no polishing the story. What happened. What it cost someone. What you'd do with the moment back. And it counts the income too: the kind word, the patience you managed, the trait you measured right. Yesterday's rabbi counted other people's buckets. Tonight's ledger counts your own.
screen: `SEARCH AND TRY OUR WAYS.` · `COME TO HESHBON: COME, ACCOUNT.` · `A SHORT REVIEW, EACH NIGHT.` · `HONEST, NOT HARSH.` · then, large: `ACCOUNT FOR THE SOUL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: review your day in two minutes. Settle, and breathe. Start from this morning and walk forward, like scrolling back through photos. Waking up. The first conversation. The middle of the day. Now. Stop at one moment that went well, and let it count. Stop at one moment you'd like back, and look at it plainly: what happened, and what it cost someone. No sentencing, no excuses. If it helps, choose the trait you've been measuring this block and look only for that. If you pray, you can bring the ledger to God in your own words. If you don't, simply close the book gently. The bell holds the time.
Cheshbon hanefesh. An accounting of the soul: an honest review of your own actions, done in Mussar practice day by day, often before sleep. Today's word.
Your line: account for the soul. Tonight, before your phone goes dark, give your day two honest minutes: one thing that counted, one you'd like back. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-four.

howItsDone: Jews traditionally make a cheshbon hanefesh in the season before Yom Kippur, and in Mussar practice it is often done briefly each night: a calm review of the day's actions, sometimes written in a notebook, focused on one trait.
